claims.text: Short-range order among the principal elements governs phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Short-range order tunes local bonding environments.
SRO-mediated phase stability can produce a microstructure that simultaneously supports high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
A two-step annealing treatment can promote higher SRO between selected element pairs in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Pair-specific bonding affinities and atomic-size differences can identify which elemental pairs should be targeted for enhanced SRO.
The extent and pattern of SRO alter local bonding and atomic packing geometry.
Enhanced SRO creates locally favorable bonding configurations.
Locally favorable bonding configurations reduce internal stresses.
Enhanced SRO stabilizes a dual-phase microstructure.
SRO-mediated microstructural tuning mitigates coarse phase separation.
Stabilization of strength-retaining phases improves high-temperature strength.
The SRO-stabilized dual-phase microstructure provides more defect sinks and thereby improves radiation tolerance.
Preventing embrittling phases improves cryogenic toughness.
Relative to the baseline, the high-SRO alloy will have a more refined and controlled dual-phase microstructure.
Relative to the baseline, the high-SRO alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the baseline, the high-SRO alloy will accumulate fewer radiation-induced defects.
Relative to the baseline, the high-SRO alloy will have greater cryogenic toughness.
The hypothesis is limited to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys whose atomic-size mismatch and electronic interactions favor SRO.
Additional alloying elements may change the bonding landscape enough that the proposed mechanism no longer applies.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements after enhancing SRO, or failure to observe the expected dual-phase distribution, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The comparison requires different annealing or heat-treatment routes to create different SRO levels, yet the conditions require equivalent thermal histories. Those requirements cannot both hold literally unless the SRO intervention is varied independently of thermal history.
